title: Media reaction: Who is to blame for COP31 ‘failure’? - Carbon Brief
gist: Carbon Brief's roundup of global media reaction to COP31 in Antalya, where at least 32 countries led by the EU and UK rejected the Turkey-Australia presidency's 'Antalya pact' cover decision for omitting fossil fuels. Blame was spread across Saudi-Russian petrostate pressure, presidency missteps and developed-country reluctance on finance, while the outcome has fuelled calls to reform the COP consensus rule. Carbon Brief notes that 'no agreement' claims are wrong, since many formal decisions were still agreed.

insights.claim: COP31 in Antalya ended without agreement on the Turkey-Australia presidency's proposed 'Antalya pact' cover decision, which at least 32 countries including the EU and UK rejected after talks overran by two days.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: No headline fossil-fuel signal from COP31 removes a policy tailwind that clean-energy narratives often lean on around summits.
insights.quote: The final text was rejected by at least 32 countries, including the EU, the UK and some climate-vulnerable countries
insights.locator: What happened at COP31?

insights.claim: Carbon Brief says media claims that COP31 ended with 'no agreement' are incorrect: the cover decision failed, but the summit still agreed many formal decisions, with progress on a phased just-transition approach and adaptation alignment.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Headline 'collapse' coverage overstates the policy damage; formal UNFCCC workstreams on just transition and adaptation continue.
insights.quote: This view, while commonly expressed in the media, is incorrect.
insights.locator: What happened at COP31?

insights.claim: Commentators blamed the COP31 presidency for pushing a cover text early in the talks instead of letting it emerge as a final synthesis of deliberations, and criticised Australian negotiations president Chris Bowen's handling of competing interests.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Process design by the host shapes summit outcomes; watch how COP32 host Ethiopia sequences its cover text.
insights.quote: thought it fit to push for a cover text early in the proceedings
insights.locator: What has the reaction to the presidency been?

insights.claim: Crikey argued Chris Bowen tried to run the global climate talks the way Australia's Labor government runs climate policy at home, quiet, pragmatic and without mentioning fossil fuels, and that this approach failed in Turkey.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Australia's domestic climate-politics approach is under reputational pressure after hosting a failed cover decision with a $150m investment.
insights.quote: quiet, pragmatic and without mentioning fossil fuels
insights.locator: What has the reaction to the presidency been?

insights.claim: Caixin commentary argued future COP presidencies should separate achievable implementation measures from ambitions that lack a coalition able to deliver them.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Signals a Chinese preference for implementation-focused rather than ambition-led COP texts, relevant to how future deals are framed.
insights.quote: distinguish achievable implementation measures from ambitions that lack a coalition capable of delivering them
insights.locator: What has the reaction to the presidency been?

themes.theme: Petrostates blamed for dropping fossil fuels

insights.claim: Much media coverage blamed oil-producing nations, led by a Saudi-Russian coalition, for the final COP31 cover decision draft containing no mention of fossil fuels or phasing out hydrocarbons.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Petrostate leverage over UN text means global fossil-fuel phase-out language remains contested, supporting the case that multilateral policy risk to hydrocarbon demand is slow-moving.
insights.quote: insisted on dropping a reference to phasing out hydrocarbons
insights.locator: How has the role of oil-rich nations been portrayed?

insights.claim: Reuters reported that negotiators from Europe, small-island states, Latin America, Asia and Africa said Saudi officials had regular access to the COP31 presidents, giving them disproportionate influence.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Points to access asymmetry as a structural channel for fossil-fuel producers to shape climate texts.
insights.quote: allowing them disproportionate influence
insights.locator: (Reuters reported that, according to negotiators

insights.claim: Michael Jacobs argued that since 'transitioning away from fossil fuels' language was included at COP28, fossil-fuel producers have been determined to ensure the phrase is never used again.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The COP28 transition language may prove a high-water mark rather than a floor, weakening expectations of escalating UN fossil-fuel commitments.
insights.quote: have been determined to ensure the phrase would never be used again
insights.locator: In Australian outlet Inside Story

insights.claim: Former BBC science editor David Shukman wrote that lobbying by oil-rich nations at UN climate talks has become increasingly blatant and aggressive over more than three decades, explaining why fossil fuels remain dominant.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Long-run evidence that the COP process has limited power to curb fossil-fuel dominance.
insights.quote: This pattern of lobbying by oil-rich nations has become increasingly blatant and aggressive over more than three decades.
insights.locator: In the i newspaper, David Shukman

insights.claim: The UAE's National framed the breakdown not as petrostate obstruction but as a failure to bridge divisions over fossil-fuel language, carbon capture and adaptation finance between major emitters, energy producers and vulnerable nations.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Gulf-aligned framing puts carbon capture and finance on par with fossil-fuel language, a narrative useful to producers defending CCS-led pathways.
insights.quote: fossil-fuel language, carbon capture and adaptation finance
insights.locator: In contrast, an editorial in the National

themes.theme: Developed nations: fossil stance vs finance gap

insights.claim: The EU, led by Irish minister Darragh O'Brien, and the UK blocked the Antalya pact because it lacked fossil-fuel language, while the US, described as the top polluter, was not present at the summit.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: With the US absent, the EU is the main developed-world force pushing fossil-fuel transition language at the UN.
insights.locator: How has the role of developed nations been portrayed?

insights.claim: Critics including a Guardian editorial said European governments were right to oppose fossil-fuel backsliding but wrong to rule out fresh EU climate funding for developing countries, with wealthy countries such as Japan, the UK and Canada aligning with the EU against long-term finance, adaptation finance and just-transition support mechanisms.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The finance standoff is the other half of the deadlock; flat developed-country climate finance constrains developing-country adaptation and transition spending.
insights.quote: they were wrong to rule out fresh EU funding for developing countries’ climate action
insights.locator: Other media outlets took a more balanced approach

insights.claim: Climate campaigner John Gibbons wrote that the EU was right to reject carbon capture and storage in the COP31 outcome.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: EU resistance to CCS in UN texts is a negative signal for CCS's political legitimacy as a climate pathway.
insights.locator: Climate campaigner John Gibbons wrote

insights.claim: India placed unusual emphasis on historical responsibility and climate finance at COP31 while playing a constructive bridging role on adaptation and just-transition texts, amid mistrust with developed countries over its opposition to fossil-fuel phaseout.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: India's stance signals continued resistance to fossil-fuel phaseout commitments without finance, relevant to coal and energy-demand outlooks there.
insights.quote: rarely with the emphasis evident
insights.locator: How has the role of developing nations been portrayed?

insights.claim: The developing-world bloc was not unified: Fiji and several other Pacific countries joined the EU and UK in refusing to endorse a compromise that avoided mentioning fossil fuels, while Kenya held firm on climate finance.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: North-south framing is too simple; climate-vulnerable states align with the EU on fossil fuels but with the global south on finance.
insights.quote: The conflict is far more complex than a mere opposition between the global north and south, or between hydrocarbon producers and consumers.
insights.locator: An editorial in the Mexican newspaper La Jornada

insights.claim: The COP31 deadlock leaves COP32 host Ethiopia to pick up the pieces.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: COP32 in Ethiopia becomes the next venue for finance and fossil-fuel language fights; watch its agenda-setting.
insights.quote: to pick up the pieces
insights.locator: Inter Press Service, a global south-focused news agency

insights.claim: Chinese state media portrayed China as a constructive defender of multilateralism at COP31, and reports said China, the African group and south-east Asian countries were willing to accept a compromise deal despite dissatisfaction with the draft text.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: China positions itself as the pragmatic dealmaker while the EU blocks, supporting its soft-power narrative in the global south.
insights.quote: willing to accept a compromise [deal] to uphold multilateralism, despite being dissatisfied with the draft text
insights.locator: Citing Chinese experts, Shanghai-based outlet the Paper

insights.claim: The Global Times rejected western calls for China to take the lead and pay, arguing that the West has unpaid climate governance arrears.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: China will not backfill developed-country climate finance gaps, keeping the finance deadlock unresolved.
insights.quote: With its own climate governance arrears unpaid, how can western media expect China to ‘pick up the tab’?
insights.locator: The Global Times editorial, meanwhile

insights.claim: China used the COP31 talks to complain about tariffs on EVs and green energy products, while its world-leading clean-technology companies featured in China pavilion events despite its diplomats keeping a low profile.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Trade friction over Chinese EVs and green products is the real economic battleground; Chinese clean-tech exporters keep advancing regardless of summit outcomes.
insights.quote: China’s clean-technology companies showed that some aspects of the green transition are persevering despite geopolitical tensions
insights.locator: Bloomberg continued

insights.claim: The European Commission is drawing up plans to overhaul the UN climate summit process because the consensus system lets a single country block an agreement among nearly 200 parties.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A move away from consensus decision-making would make petrostate vetoes less effective and could speed fossil-fuel transition language; watch the reform push.
insights.quote: a single country can block an agreement among nearly 200 parties
insights.locator: What does this mean for the consensus process and reform?

insights.claim: Reform proposals floated for COPs include shortening the conference from two weeks, limiting it to delegates and reducing its size, with commentators comparing COP31 to the 2009 Copenhagen failure that preceded the Paris Agreement.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Historical precedent suggests summit failures can trigger architectural reinvention rather than permanent stalling.
insights.quote: Following the defeat, negotiators went back to the drawing board and created the architecture that led to the Paris Agreement.
insights.locator: Justin Worland, a senior correspondent at Time

insights.claim: Some commentators, including Bill Hare, Johan Rockström and a Bloomberg editorial, framed the rejection as a positive signal: more than 100 governments, led by the EU, opposed a declaration that omitted the transition away from fossil fuels.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A majority bloc willing to reject weak texts may push 'coalitions of the willing' outside the consensus process, a channel for faster policy action.
insights.quote: More than 100 governments, led by the EU, opposed a final declaration
insights.locator: Could COP31 send a ‘positive signal’?
